channel.title: Oddly Wired
channel.description: One checked psychology fact a day. Every claim names the study behind it.

item.title: You are remarkably good at ignoring what you do not want to see.
item.description: Selective perception allows individuals to interpret ambiguous actions differently to align with partisan interests, a phenomenon demonstrated in the 1954 study 'They Saw a Game' by Hastorf and Cantril.

item.title: You assume people are consistent even when they are not.
item.description: The 'Correspondence Bias' leads you to attribute behavior to personality rather than the situation.

item.title: The complexity of a task makes you procrastinate less.
item.description: Parkinson's Law of Triviality states that the time spent on any item of an agenda is in inverse proportion to the amount of money involved.

item.title: Your brain prefers a world with simple, rigid categories.
item.description: Psychological essentialism leads you to believe that objects and people have an underlying, unchanging nature.

item.title: You use your own life as the ultimate metric.
item.description: The 'Curse of Knowledge' describes your tendency to over-rely on your own perspective when judging the knowledge of others.

item.title: You support systems that reinforce your own group's dominance.
item.description: Social Dominance Orientation measures your preference for hierarchical group relations over equality.

item.title: Your attention is silently pulled toward what you fear.
item.description: An attentional bias causes the mind to demonstrate an initial orientation toward threat-related stimuli before conscious awareness.

item.title: Venting your anger makes you more aggressive, not less.
item.description: A 2002 study showed that participants who hit a punching bag to vent anger were more aggressive than those who sat quietly.

item.title: Your brain expects others to help carry your burdens.
item.description: Social Baseline Theory suggests the human brain perceives the world as requiring less effort when a social partner is present.

item.title: You misremember when events in your life actually happened.
item.description: The telescoping effect causes people to shift distant events forward in time and recent events further back.

item.title: You prefer a known failure to an unknown outcome.
item.description: Humans tend to prefer smaller, guaranteed payoffs over larger, uncertain ones in the domain of gains, but often favor risk when facing potential losses.

item.title: You are more likely to lie when you feel moral.
item.description: Mazar and Zhong (2010) found that individuals who performed or recalled virtuous actions, such as buying eco-friendly products, were subsequently more likely to cheat, a phenomenon termed moral licensing.

item.title: You assign value to objects solely through ownership.
item.description: A 1991 study found individuals value their own items at approximately twice the price (a 100% increase) they are willing to pay for an identical item.

item.title: Your focus defines the limits of your reality.
item.description: The bottleneck model of attention suggests you process only a fraction of available sensory input.

item.title: Your senses shut down to save energy over time.
item.description: Sensory adaptation occurs when your receptors decrease their response to constant, unchanging stimulation.

item.title: You perceive motion even when nothing is moving.
item.description: The phi phenomenon is a distinct perceptual illusion of 'objectless' motion, whereas the illusion of motion in film (where a figure appears to travel between two points) is known as beta movement.

item.title: Your baseline for intelligence has shifted over the decades.
item.description: The Flynn effect describes the observed rise in raw IQ scores throughout the 20th century.

item.title: Your internal criteria decide what is signal and noise.
item.description: Signal detection theory posits that your response criterion depends on your current decision threshold.

item.title: Distance alters your perception of size without your consent.
item.description: Mario Ponzo first demonstrated the illusion in 1911.

item.title: Repeating a word eventually makes it lose all meaning.
item.description: The verbal transformation effect is a perceptual phenomenon where continuous repetition of a word causes a listener to experience shifts in perception, leading them to report hearing different words.

item.title: Small changes are invisible against large existing quantities.
item.description: Weber’s Law states that the just-noticeable difference in a stimulus is proportional to its intensity.

item.title: Your brain fills in gaps to create complete objects.
item.description: The Law of Closure describes how the mind perceives incomplete figures as complete, coherent wholes.

item.title: You are happier when you stay busy.
item.description: In a 2010 study, participants who were assigned a task were significantly happier when they had to perform it, even if the task was tedious, than when they were left idle.

item.title: You view your past through your present.
item.description: Research on 'hindsight bias' shows that after an outcome is revealed, people consistently overestimate their past ability to predict it.

item.title: Writing your worries down fixes your focus.
item.description: In a 2011 study, college students who wrote about their anxieties before an exam performed significantly better than those who did not.

item.title: Context changes the emotion you read in others.
item.description: The Kuleshov effect demonstrates that film audiences attribute different emotions to an identical facial expression based on the preceding scene.

item.title: A clean smell makes you more generous.
item.description: In a 2010 study, participants in a room sprayed with all-purpose cleaner were significantly more likely to volunteer for a charitable task than those in a non-scented room.

item.title: You are a different person in different rooms.
item.description: Research by Mark Snyder in 1974 found that individuals possess distinct levels of self-monitoring, where some constantly adapt their persona to fit the situation.

item.title: You cannot stop yourself from imagining an impossible scenario.
item.description: Counterfactual thinking is your brain's persistent attempt to simulate 'what if' scenarios to understand outcomes.

item.title: You judge people by their actions, but yourself by intent.
item.description: Research suggests the actor-observer asymmetry is highly context-dependent rather than a universal cognitive bias.

item.title: New memories actively overwrite what you already remembered.
item.description: Retroactive interference describes the inhibition or competitive interference that makes it difficult to retrieve older memories due to the acquisition of new, similar information.

item.title: You cannot find the word you know you know.
item.description: The tip-of-the-tongue state represents a partial retrieval failure where you access the definition but not the label.

item.title: Your focus on a weapon blinds you to everything else.
item.description: When a weapon is present during a crime, witnesses remember fewer details about the perpetrator and the scene.

item.title: Your brain blocks out memories to clear the way.
item.description: Proactive interference occurs when your older memories disrupt your ability to recall newer information.

item.title: You claim to know things that do not exist.
item.description: When presented with lists containing fictional concepts, many people claim they are familiar with them.

item.title: Speaking two languages physically reorganizes your brain's efficiency.
item.description: Some studies suggest that bilingual individuals may demonstrate an advantage in specific executive function tasks, though this remains a subject of intense scientific debate and is not considered a universally established fact.

item.title: You value information simply because a successful person said it.
item.description: Prestige bias is the tendency to assign greater weight to the opinions of people who are high-status, regardless of their expertise in the specific topic.

item.title: The faster your city, the less likely you are to help.
item.description: A 1999 study of 31 cities found a correlation between an aggregate 'pace of life' index—which included walking speed, work speed, and public clock accuracy—and the likelihood to assist a stranger.

item.title: You believe every category has a hidden, unchanging truth.
item.description: Psychological essentialism explains your tendency to assume that groups—like gender or race—possess an immutable, internal 'essence'.

item.title: You fail to reach goals by ignoring obstacles ahead.
item.description: Mental contrasting demonstrates that visualizing success without anticipating specific obstacles actually reduces your goal-directed energy.

item.title: You remember the punchline far better than the context.
item.description: Research indicates that information presented in a humorous way is often recalled better than neutral information, though this effect is moderated by the relevance of the humor to the content.

item.title: You overestimate your personal consistency.
item.description: The 'end of history illusion' suggests that people consistently fail to anticipate how their personality and preferences will shift over time.

item.title: You don't know what you want until you see it.
item.description: Preference construction theory demonstrates that people do not have fixed internal values; instead, they build their preferences in the moment of choice.

item.title: You value things more when they are scarce.
item.description: Research shows that participants in a 1975 study rated identical items as significantly more valuable simply because they were told supply was limited.

item.title: You underestimate how much control you have over your habits.
item.description: Research indicates that people who view willpower as a limited resource perform worse on self-control tasks than those who don't.

item.title: You are more creative when the font is harder to read.
item.description: Cognitive disfluency—the experience of difficulty in processing information—can trigger more deliberate, analytic thinking.

item.title: You see yourself as less capable than you are.
item.description: When tasks are difficult, people consistently exhibit a worse-than-average effect, underestimating their relative performance.

item.title: Your brain ignores most of the visual world.
item.description: Change blindness results suggest that visual perception is not a continuous, high-definition recording, highlighting the dependency of visual awareness on focused attention.

item.title: You value things more just because you made them.
item.description: The IKEA effect demonstrates that people assign higher value to projects or products when they have personally contributed to their creation.

item.title: You fear losing more than you value gaining.
item.description: Prospect theory suggests that the psychological pain of losing $100 is roughly twice as intense as the pleasure of gaining $100.
